title: Chapter 177 – Qinghe's Kitchen
html:
[The Garden Hall, Great Kitchen – Qinghe]

The kettle is the first thing Qinghe checks every morning, and on the third morning of the siege it is still hot.

She notices this the way she notices most things now, with her hand and not her tongue. She lays two fingers on the black iron belly of it, where the soot has worn through to a dull shine, and feels the warmth come up into her knuckles. It is a hundred years old, that kettle. It came into the Garden on a mule, wrapped in a quilt, when she was a bride of nineteen and the Lin clan had eleven members and a goat. It has boiled water for weddings and for wakes. It has never once gone cold on her.

"Mistress," says the girl at her elbow. "The rice."

"I know about the rice."

"There isn't enough."

"There is never enough." Qinghe turns. "How much?"

"We have the big bin, and the two small ones, and the sack from the cellar." The girl is sixteen, round-faced, flour to the elbows, and she is trying very hard to sound steady. Her name is Pia. She was a scullion until a week ago. "Cook Feng says it will feed three thousand for four days. Perhaps five if we thin it."

"Then we thin it." Qinghe lifts the lid of the big pot and looks in. Steam rolls up into her face. She breathes it in, deeply, because she can still smell, and the smell is rice and ginger and a trace of wood smoke, and under all of that the faint sourness of too many people in too small a space. "Is the porridge salted?"

"Yes, Mistress."

"Taste it."

Pia dips a spoon and blows on it and tastes, and her eyes go thoughtful. "Not enough."

"Not enough." Qinghe nods. "Add a pinch. Not two. If I'm wrong, you tell me. If you're right, tell me anyway."

She does not say the rest: that she cannot tell herself. That she has not tasted salt in twenty years. That the knack she once had is gone from her tongue, and she has made herself a new one out of the faces of the people eating, and the small shy honesty of a girl with a spoon.

Pia adds a pinch. Qinghe watches her do it, and thinks, as she has thought every morning for a week: Someone should be teaching her this. Someone has to be left to teach her.

She sets the thought aside, like a dish she is not ready to wash, and goes to see about the bread.

* * *

The Great Kitchen was built to feed four hundred, and tonight it is feeding three thousand.

They came up from the lower terraces on the first night, and from the villages along the river, and from the orchard hands' cottages that are now holes in the ground. Old men with bundles. Women with babies. Children asleep on their feet. Zhao ordered the Hall opened, every cellar and chamber and corridor, and by the second dusk there was not a floor in the Garden without a body on it. They lie in rows in the great hall under the lamp-beams. They lie in the corridors, in the archives, in the cold pantries, in the chapel of the First Gate-Keeper, where an old man snores gently beneath the carved lintel.

And every one of them wants feeding.

Qinghe has not slept for two nights. She does not intend to. She moves through the kitchen with her sleeves rolled and her white hair bound in a wet cloth, giving orders in a voice that has not been raised since the year the roof fell in. Eighty women and boys work under her, chopping and stirring and hauling. They do not talk much. There is a long silence in the Great Kitchen, a fierce intent silence, broken only by the knock of knives and the roar of the ovens.

The ovens are the heart of it. There are nine, built into the thick north wall, each as big as a cart, each fed from a stoke-hole on the outer side. They have been lit continuously since the siege began. The heat is a living presence in the room, a wall of dry gold, and the faces of the women are slick and flushed. Qinghe likes it. She has always liked it. A kitchen should be too hot.

"Mistress Qinghe." A boy runs up, one of the stokers, black to the eyebrows. "The Clan Head wants you in the hall."

"Now?"

"She said now."

Qinghe wipes her hands. She looks round once at the ovens, at the girl with the spoon, at the great black kettle steaming on its hook in the hearth.

"Keep that on," she says, to nobody. "If it goes cold, I will know."

* * *

Zhao is sitting at the long table in the council room with a map under her elbows and her husband's hand in hers.

He is not well. That is the first thing Qinghe sees, and it is a shock, though she has known it for a month. Old Dao has been the clan's quartermaster for sixty years: a square, gentle, humorous man who kept the winter stores like a miser and the festival wine like a priest. He is lying on a cot beside the table now, under three blankets, with his face the color of candle wax and his breath coming in shallow rasps. His fingers move a little on his wife's. His eyes are closed.

"He sleeps," says Zhao. "The healer says it is only weariness."

"The healer is a liar."

"Yes." Zhao smiles without humor. She is past eighty. She has been Clan Head for thirty years, and in all that time she has never looked as she does now: bent, stripped, burning with a dry bright resolve. "Sit, Qinghe. I need your opinion, and I need it fast."

Qinghe sits. On the table lies a plan of the Garden, hand-drawn on rice paper, with the Hall at its heart and the wards marked in red. Three of the red lines have been crossed out.

"The north wards are failing," says Zhao. "Ning Ruiyan's observatory went in the night. Lu Fei's array-markers on the lower terraces are gone. The only thing keeping the beasts out of the Hall's west cellars is the stair, and Tian Mo has the stair." She pauses. "Or had it, an hour ago. I have had no word since."

"I heard."

"What did you hear?"

"That he's alive," says Qinghe. "That the roots saved him. That he lost an arm."

Zhao closes her eyes briefly. "Then he has lost an arm and not his life. I will take that." She opens them again. "Qinghe, I have a plan. I do not like it. I would like you to tell me why it is wrong."

"Tell me the plan."

"Darkness."

Qinghe stares at her.

"The beasts come for light," says Zhao. "That is my reading. You have seen the orchard. They came out of the ground at dusk, when every lamp in the Garden was lit. They tore through the lit places first. The Hall is a beacon, a great bright lantern on the hill, and everything below us is drawn to it." She sweeps a hand over the map. "I want the Hall dark. Every lamp out. Every hearth banked. Every window shuttered. Let the beasts find nothing but a black hill, and perhaps they will pass us by."

Qinghe says nothing for a moment. She thinks of the Great Kitchen, with its nine roaring ovens. She thinks of three thousand people lying in their rows in the warm yellow dusk.

"They would freeze," she says.

"It is autumn, not winter."

"It is autumn in the mountains. There are children in the lower corridors who cannot be warmed with blankets." Qinghe leans forward. "And the porridge, Zhao. I cannot cook rice in the dark. I cannot bake bread with the ovens banked. In two days they would be hungry as well as cold."

"Better hungry than dead."

"Is that the choice?"

"I do not know." Zhao's voice drops. "I do not know, Qinghe. That is why I sent for you. I am eighty-two years old and I have no idea what I am doing. Every plan I make costs lives. I need someone to tell me which cost is smaller."

Qinghe looks at her for a long moment. Then she reaches across the table, and takes the old woman's free hand, and holds it.

"The beasts came to the orchard at dusk," she says. "When the lamps were lit."

"Yes."

"And the stair. When did they come to the stair?"

"The second hour of the night."

"With the lamps lit?"

"The stair lamps are blue," says Zhao slowly. "They were failing. Half of them were out."

"Out." Qinghe taps the table. "And Pia's report from the lower cellar this morning? The children in the north corridor, where we have no hearth. They said something came scratching at the door in the night."

Zhao's face goes very still.

"I do not think they come for the light," Qinghe says. "I think they come for the dark."

* * *

It takes her an hour to be sure.

She does it the way she does most things, by asking the people who know. She goes down into the cellars with a lamp and a boy to carry it, and she talks to the guards at the doors, and the women in the corridors, and the old men in the archives. She asks one question over and over: Where did the sounds come from? Where did they scratch?

The answers are the same.

They came to the dark places. The northeast pantry, where the lamps had burned out. The cold stairwell by the old well, where nobody had thought to put a light. The north corridor, where the children slept in the black. They came to a door, and scratched, and waited, and in three places they got through. And in every case, as the guards tell it, when someone ran up with a torch, the thing in the doorway stopped, and shook its blind head, and backed away.

"It flinched," says an old man in the archive, with great satisfaction. "Like a cat from a hot stove. I saw it myself."

Qinghe stands in the dim passage with the lamp in her hand and does the sum.

It is the same thing, she thinks. The thing that came for the shed terraces. The thing Bell said came for the dark. They are drawn to the places where the light has failed, because that is where the sleepers are weakest, and the Hall's dark is the Hall's wound. She does not understand the whole of it. She is a cook. But she knows the shape of it, as she knows the shape of a loaf rising: a dull heavy pressure from below, a hunger that goes toward the soft place.

So we do not hide in the dark. We make there be no dark.

She turns and goes back up the stairs at a speed that terrifies the boy with the lamp.

* * *

"No," says Zhao.

"Yes."

"We have two thousand pounds of lamp oil and four hundred of lard. If we light every lamp in the Hall, we will burn through it in three nights."

"Then we burn through it in three nights."

"And on the fourth?"

"On the fourth, either the siege is over or it isn't." Qinghe plants both hands on the table. "I have thought about it, Zhao. I have thought about every way it could go wrong. You can hide the Hall in the dark, and watch them find the north corridor, and the cold stairwell, and the children. Or you can burn the oil. It will cost us the winter. I am old enough to know what that means, and still I say: burn it."

Zhao searches her face. She is trembling very slightly. Then, abruptly, she laughs, a short cracked laugh.

"You cooked for my wedding," she says. "Do you remember? The whole chicken. I was so frightened that I could not eat, and you stood over me with a spoon and said, You will be a bad bride if you faint."

"I remember."

"I did not faint." Zhao wipes her eyes. "Burn it, Qinghe. Every lamp in the Hall. And light the ovens beyond that, and stoke the hearths, and tell the pupils to carry torches down the corridors. Let it be festival night." She hesitates. "And tell Feng to bring the drums."

"The drums?"

"If it is to be festival night, let us have the noise of one."

* * *

Feng finds her in the pantry, counting lamps.

He is ninety, bent like a question mark, and he has been telling the story of the goat for as long as anyone alive can remember. He leans in the doorway with a drumstick in one fist and a half-eaten bun in the other, and his eyes, which see everything in the Garden and remember none of it in order, are bright with a strange hard clarity.

"Seventy-one," Qinghe says, not looking up. "In the east pantry. I have forty more on the shelf. Where am I going to find the rest?"

"The chapel."

"What?"

"The old man in the chapel. He has a night-lamp the size of a bucket, I saw it. And the First Gate-Keeper's shrine has a hundred votive lamps, little clay ones, they have been sitting there for two hundred years." He points the drumstick at her. "Light those."

"They are offerings."

"They are lamps." He grins. "You know what the First Gate-Keeper said? When they asked him what the shrine was for? He said, a place to keep the dark away. I read it in the archive when I was a boy. I thought it was poetry." He shakes his head, wondering. "Fifty years, I have walked past those lamps. And I never once thought they meant it."

Qinghe puts down her tally-stick.

"Feng," she says. "How do you feel?"

"Like a drum." He laughs, and the laugh turns into a cough, and she watches him bend over the doorpost until it passes. He straightens. His eyes are wet. "I heard it, Qinghe. In the night. The thing in the wall. It is not a sound, you know. It is a shape. It is like a very large person, very far away, turning over in his sleep."

"Do not talk about it."

"Why not? It is the most interesting thing that has happened to me since the goat." He finishes the bun. "Go and get the lamps. I will take the drums down to the cellars. We will make such a racket they will hear it in the capital."

She watches him go, lurching down the corridor with the stick under his arm, and thinks that if the world ends tomorrow, she will have been allowed to see Feng happy. It is a small thing. She files it away with the others.

* * *

She goes to see Yue before she lights the shrine.

The girl, who is not a girl, is seventy-one, and deaf, and she sits on a stool in the lower chamber with her back against the Gate-door and her hand resting flat on a gray stone no bigger than a loaf. The Pebble. It is dull and cracked and cold. Beside her, on a blanket, Lin Kuang lies asleep with his sword across his chest and his mouth open. Qinghe tucks the blanket under his chin.

Yue turns her head. Her face is thin and fine and very calm. She raises one hand and makes a small shape in the air, the sign for tea, and Qinghe smiles and shakes her head, and sets down the kettle on the stone floor between them.

Hot, she signs, with the two fingers Yue taught her in the spring. Warm. Drink.

Yue pours. She does it with the grave care of a woman handling something holy. She holds the cup out, and Qinghe takes it, and the two of them sit together in the thick quiet, an old cook and an old deaf woman, with a cracked stone between them that is holding a door against the end of the world.

Heavy? Qinghe signs at last, tapping the Pebble.

Yue considers. Then she nods, slowly, and her free hand lifts to her ear, and makes a gesture Qinghe has not seen before: a circle, closing. And she points at the ceiling, and the Hall above them, and the fire.

Qinghe blinks.

The lights, she signs back. You can feel the lights?

A smile. Yue puts her palm on the Pebble and closes her eyes, and a look comes over her face of deep, sleepy relief, like a woman sinking into a hot bath. It is the look of someone who has been bearing a weight on her back for three days, and has just felt a hand take the corner.

Qinghe sits very still with the cup in her hands, and feels, for the first time in a long while, the happiness of being right.

* * *

The chapel of the First Gate-Keeper is a small low room smelling of dust and cold wax, and it takes eleven children and a taper to wake it.

Qinghe has gathered them from the corridor: eleven of the smallest, the ones too young to carry water and too restless to sleep. She lines them up before the shrine, where a hundred little clay lamps sit on a black stone ledge, each no bigger than an egg-cup, each full of oil that has not been touched in a generation. The wicks are brittle. Some have crumbled to powder. She shows the children how to pinch a fresh thread from her own sleeve and twist it, and how to set it in the oil, and how to hold the taper without letting the flame touch the fingers.

"One each," she says. "Go slowly. Do not burn yourselves."

"Why are we doing this, Granny?" asks a small boy named Tuo.

"Because someone, a long time ago, said the dark should be kept away. And we are going to find out whether he meant it."

"Is it magic?"

"It is oil," says Qinghe. "And a wick. And a child's patient hand. In my experience, that is all the magic there is."

They go to work. The little flames come up one at a time, yellow and quivering, until the whole ledge glows, and the carved face of the First Gate-Keeper above it, rough, plain, with a deep line between the brows, seems to look down on them with something very like approval. The old man by the lintel has woken. He watches the children with his mouth open.

Tuo lights the last lamp. He turns to Qinghe, his small face solemn in the glow, and asks, "Does it work?"

She does not answer at once. She is listening.

Somewhere deep under the floor, far below the cellars, below the Gate-door and the Pebble and the sleeping stone, there is a sound she has never heard before. It is not a voice. It is not a beast. It is a long slow exhalation, the sound a very large creature makes when it lets go of a breath it has been holding for years.

"Yes," she says. "I think so."

* * *

By midnight the Garden Hall is lit like a lantern fair.

Qinghe walks the length of it with the black kettle in her hand, because she has not been able to put it down, and she sees the work of her people in every window. Oil lamps on every sill. Rush torches in every corridor. The great hall blazing with a hundred hanging lanterns, and the cold stairwell lit with a ring of candles stuck in melted wax on the stones. Children sleep in pools of gold. The old man in the chapel has been given a night-lamp the size of his head, which he regards with wary delight.

And from the west cellars, faint, through two floors of stone, there comes the sound of the drums.

Feng has gathered them. Twenty of the Garden's old festival drums, dragged out of their store-room, thumped by cooks and farmers and boys of eleven with a ferocious joy. It is not music. It is a deep, uneven, rattling thunder, passing from cellar to cellar like a heartbeat. Tum. Tum-tum. Tum. Qinghe feels it in the soles of her feet. Beside her, Pia is swaying a little, her eyes closed.

"Is it working?" the girl whispers.

"I don't know."

They climb to the west tower and look out.

The night is black. The Garden spreads below, a dark rumpled sea of terraces, and in the midst of it the Hall sits on its hill like a lit coal. Beyond the outer wall, on the lower ground, the tide of crawlers is moving. Qinghe can see it now: a faint pale glimmer in the dark, a slow crawling ripple like the surface of a lake. It is coming up the hill.

It comes. And comes. It reaches the base of the first terrace, a dark pale mass a mile wide, and begins to climb.

"Oh," says Pia.

"Hold my hand," says Qinghe.

The tide climbs the second terrace. The third. It is nearly at the outer wall when the light from the Hall's long windows falls across the leading edge of it, and Qinghe sees the first crawler lift its blind head, and hesitate.

It checks. Behind it, another checks. A ripple runs back through the whole advancing mass, like the shiver that runs through a herd. They bunch. They mill. For a moment the entire tide seems to stand quite still on the slope below the Hall, a lake of pale flesh turned toward the light.

Then they begin to turn.

They do not retreat. They slide, sideways, a great slow shearing movement, away from the lit terraces and toward the dark places on either side: the old orchard, the sunken lane, the ruined well-house, the drainage gullies between the hills. They flow around the lit Hall as water flows around a stone. And what they leave behind, in the glow of a thousand lamps, is a long slope of empty ground.

Pia is crying. Qinghe is not. She stands with her hand locked on the girl's and the great black kettle hanging heavy from the other, and she watches the tide of the dark pass the Hall by.

"We did it," whispers Pia. "Mistress. We did it."

"No." Qinghe's voice is hoarse. "We only moved it."

She looks at the pale tide streaming off toward the north and the east, away from the Hall, toward whatever stands there in the dark. She sees where it is going. She sees the long, thin, glimmering line of the Valley Wall, two miles of it, and the Sect banners above, and the blue wards flaring, and the dark places along it where the lamps are few.

We lit the Hall, she thinks, and the Wall is still dark.

Behind her, in the stairwell, a boy is running up the steps with a torch and a word from the Clan Head, shouting it before he reaches the top.

"Mistress Qinghe! Mistress! It's the Head's order!" He skids to a halt, gasping. "She says, Take the lamps to the Wall. All of them. Every spare lantern, every drum, every pot of oil. She says the Wall is going to need to be a festival too."

Qinghe closes her eyes.

Three nights of oil, she thinks. And now we are giving it away.

"Tell her yes," she says. "Tell her the kitchen will send the first cart at dawn."

She turns, kettle in hand, and starts down the stairs to begin loading.
